item.title: Depleting Nucleation: Out-of-Equilibrium Effects of Monomer Consumption and System Adiabaticity on the Activation Energy Barrier
item.description:
This work challenges two common assumptions of Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT), namely, isothermal conditions and a constant supply of monomers, which can lead to inaccuracies in predicting nucleation rates in small, well-insulated systems. Given the contemporary focus on synthesizing nanoparticles and nanocrystals for various industrial applications, a re-examination of how these factors impact the activation energy of nucleation is warranted. A more accurate relationship is proposed to account for the selfheating that occurs in thermally insulated systems. Furthermore, to address the effect of monomer consumption by cluster formation, the Gibbs-Thomson equation is incorporated into the existing theoretical framework to describe the increase in the activation energy that accompanies supersaturation relief. The newly proposed equation simultaneously helps reconcile the recent observation that the CNT-predicted energy barrier is systematically underestimated by a factor of approximately 1.78 [Skrdla, P. J. "A Theoretical Approach for Modeling Non-steady-state Nucleation Kinetics in Solutions and Melts." J. Phys. Chem. C 130 (2026): 3614–3623]. Although the condensation of water is used as a case study, the methodologies presented are broadly applicable to any nucleating system operating under the constraints of finite volume and adiabaticity.

Peter J. Skrdla

item.title: Surface Geometry Governs Cation Effects via Nonlocal Solvent Gating
item.description:
Catalyst structure and electrolyte composition are commonly regarded as independent descriptors governing electrocatalytic behavior. Here, we show that surface geometry governs cation effects through catalyst–electrolyte coupling that we term nonlocal solvent gating. Constant-potential ab initio molecular dynamics simulations and free-energy sampling reveal contrasting cation (Li+, K+, Cs+)-dependent CO2 reduction activity on single-crystal and polycrystalline Au. On relatively flat Au(100) and Au(111), cation hydration controls the contact-water structure, and the solvent penalty for CO2 approach decreases with increasing cation size. In Au(110) grooves, surface-registered water instead reverses the cation response. Remarkably, an Au(110)-like groove embedded within an otherwise flat Au(111) terrace induces the same reversed cation trend even at geometrically pristine terrace sites away from the groove, demonstrating that a local surface motif can regulate electrolyte effects nonlocally through the interfacial solvent. An additional calculation for Rb+ supports this mechanism, yielding an intermediate groove-induced cavity penalty. This nonlocal coupling provides a mechanistic basis for the experimentally observed volcano-shaped cation dependence on flame-annealed polycrystalline Au, which cannot be explained by independent single-facet responses. These results establish interfacial water as a medium through which surface geometry and electrolyte composition become intrinsically coupled, extending conventional local-site descriptions of complex electrocatalytic interfaces to include nonlocal solvent-mediated effects.

Xiao Ma, Leshen Zhang, Guangsheng Liu, Abdulrahman Allangawi, Huabin Zhang, Wan-Lu Li

item.title: Vacancy-Controlled Stabilization and Reactivity of Single Metal Atoms on Titanium Nitride and Titanium Oxynitride
item.description:
Titanium nitride (TiN) and titanium oxynitride (TiON) are attractive conductive supports for single-atom electrocatalysts, but the role of surface vacancies in balancing metal stabilization and catalytic reactivity remains unclear. Here, we used density functional theory to screen the formation of Ag, Au, Co, Cu, Ir, Ni, Pd, Pt, Rh, and Ru single atoms on pristine and vacancy-containing TiN and TiON surfaces, and their reactivity toward the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Vacancy formation generally strengthens single-atom anchoring, but the corresponding changes in hydrogen adsorption are strongly metal- and defect-dependent, showing that a stronger metal–support interaction does not necessarily imply improved HER activity. Combining hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics with electrochemical dissolution stability identifies Pd atoms trapped in Ti vacancies (VTi) as the most promising candidates. Importantly, Pd@VTi shows nearly identical hydrogen adsorption energetics and dissolution potentials above 0 V vs. SHE for TiN and both investigated TiON configurations, indicating remarkable insensitivity to the local O/N arrangement. Electronic-structure analysis, ab initio molecular dynamics, and surface Pourbaix calculations further support the viability of these configurations. These results highlight cation-vacancy-confined Pd as a robust HER motif on compositionally variable Ti(O)N supports.

Lazar Bijelic, Ana S. Dobrota, Natalia V. Skorodumova, Igor A. Pašti

item.title: IntelliPore: A Foundation Model for Gas Adsorption in Porous Materials
item.description:
Porous materials, such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and zeolites, hold great promise for energy and environmental applications, particularly in gas storage and separation technologies. However, their rapidly expanding design space, driven by experimental synthesis and computational modeling, challenges traditional exploration methods. Machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative, yet current approaches are typically developed for specific adsorption properties or material families. Consequently, each new property or material class requires training a new model from scratch using large amounts of labeled data, which are often not available. Inspired by the emerging foundation-model paradigm that has transformed computer vision and natural language processing, we introduce IntelliPore, a foundation model tailored for gas adsorption in porous materials. By pretraining on 12.5 million publicly available adsorption data from MOFs and COFs, IntelliPore learns transferable knowledge across adsorption tasks and material classes, enabling generalization to previously unseen materials such as zeolites and porous polymer networks. It demonstrates strong few-shot learning capabilities, substantially improving sample efficiency compared with the traditional approach of training from scratch. Furthermore, it achieves state-of-the-art performance in adsorption property prediction with exceptional parameter efficiency, requiring only 0.86 million parameters—two orders of magnitude fewer than existing leading models. To facilitate broader adoption, IntelliPore is made publicly available to the research community and accessible through a web application. Collectively, these advances establish IntelliPore as a practical foundation for data-driven adsorption modeling in porous materials and represent a step toward the emerging paradigm of foundation-style models in materials science.

Antonios P. Sarikas, George E. Froudakis

item.title: A Gentle Push: Fine-Tuning Foundation Models for Complex Oxide Surface Reconstructions
item.description:
Structure-prediction methods routinely sample highly distorted, far-from-equilibrium configurations. Conventional workflows based on machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) therefore require the inclusion of unphysical local atomic environments in the training data to ensure stability during the search. We show that foundation MLIPs, fine-tuned on minimal datasets containing only physically reasonable structures, can serve as robust backbones for evolutionary structure prediction of complex surface reconstructions. We systematically benchmark fine-tuning strategies and identify that freezing all layers except the readouts as the most effective strategy in the low-data regime. Fine-tuning on as few as 23 structures is sufficient to perform evolutionary searches on reconstructed SrTiO 3 (110) surfaces. For BaTiO 3 (001), we further demonstrate that a lightweight active-learning approach, based on fine-tuning on as few as 20 structures, enables the identification of new low-energy (√5 × √5)R26.6° reconstructions.

Ralf Wanzenböck, Eva Doloszeski, Georg K. H. Madsen
